los.text: Know epidemiology, pathophysiology and common presentation and relate to structure and function of skin.
los.html:
• Epidemiology: skin disease is very common (around a quarter of people consult their GP about skin each year)
    • the commonest problems are eczema, psoriasis, acne, skin infections, urticaria and skin cancer (BCC is the most common cancer in the UK).
LayerStructureFunction → disease
EpidermisStratified squamous keratinising epithelium (basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum); keratinocytes, melanocytes, Langerhans cells, Merkel cells
  • Barrier (lipids, filaggrin, tight junctions) → eczema
  • Turnover ~28 days → psoriasis
  • Melanin UV protection → skin cancer, vitiligo
  • Immune sentinel → contact dermatitis
Basement membrane zoneHemidesmosomes, anchoring fibrilsAdhesion → pemphigoid (subepidermal blisters)
DermisCollagen, elastin, fibroblasts, blood vessels, nerves, adnexa (hair follicles, sebaceous, eccrine, apocrine glands), mast cellsStrength, thermoregulation (vessels, sweat), sensation → urticaria, vasculitis, acne, itch
SubcutisFatInsulation, energy, cushioning → panniculitis (erythema nodosum)
  • Other functions: vitamin D synthesis, communication and appearance (psychological impact). Loss of all functions = skin failure (erythroderma, TEN).

los.text: Assess and diagnose patients with dermatological disease and formulate initial management plan.
los.html:
StepDetail
History
  • Onset
  • Duration
  • Site
  • Evolution
  • Symptoms (itch, pain)
  • Triggers
  • Treatments tried
  • PMH (atopy)
  • Drugs (new drugs in the last 8 weeks)
  • Allergies
  • Family history (atopy, psoriasis, melanoma)
  • Occupation (wet work, contact allergens)
  • Sun exposure
  • Travel
  • Contacts
  • Impact (sleep, work, mood: DLQI)
Examination
  • Whole skin in good light
  • Distribution, configuration, morphology (see ICM Year 2 › Skin & lumps › LO 1)
  • Palpate
  • Hair, nails, mucosae, lymph nodes
  • Dermatoscopy
Investigations
  • Swabs (bacteria, viral PCR)
  • Skin scrapings and nail clippings (fungi)
  • Biopsy (punch, shave, excision; direct immunofluorescence for blistering)
  • Patch testing (allergic contact dermatitis)
  • Bloods
Initial management
  • Emollients for dry skin, topical steroids of the right potency, antimicrobials for infection, avoid triggers
  • Systemic treatment, phototherapy or referral if severe
  • Suspected cancer pathway for suspected melanoma or SCC

los.text: Know the possibility of comorbidities such as psoriatic arthritis and metabolic syndrome.
los.html:
Skin diseaseComorbidities
Psoriasis
  • Psoriatic arthritis (~20–30%: screen yearly with PEST)
  • Metabolic syndrome (obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension)
  • Cardiovascular disease (severe psoriasis raises MI risk)
  • NAFLD
  • IBD
  • Depression and anxiety
  • Alcohol and smoking
  • Uveitis
Atopic eczemaAsthma, allergic rhinitis, food allergy ("atopic march"), sleep loss, depression
Hidradenitis suppurativaObesity, metabolic syndrome, IBD, depression
AcneLow mood, PCOS
  • Why it matters: chronic systemic inflammation drives comorbidity
    • holistic care includes CV risk assessment (QRISK), weight, smoking and alcohol support, joint review and mental health
    • some drugs treat both skin and joints (methotrexate, biologics).

los.text: Know the structure and function of normal skin and relate this knowledge to alterations in the context of disease.
los.html:
Normal structure/functionAlteration in disease
Epidermal turnover ~28 daysPsoriasis: ~3–5 days → thick scaly plaques
Filaggrin and stratum corneum lipids form the barrierAtopic eczema, ichthyosis vulgaris (filaggrin mutations) → dry skin, allergen and microbe entry
Desmosomes (desmogleins 1 and 3) hold keratinocytes togetherPemphigus (anti-desmoglein): intraepidermal, flaccid blisters; SSSS (toxin cleaves desmoglein 1)
Hemidesmosomes (BP180, BP230) anchor the basal layerBullous pemphigoid: subepidermal, tense blisters
Melanocytes make melaninVitiligo (destroyed), melanoma (malignant), melasma (overactive)
Langerhans cells present antigenAllergic contact dermatitis (type IV)
Dermal collagen and elastinAgeing and photoageing (solar elastosis), scleroderma (fibrosis), striae (steroids)
Mast cells and vesselsUrticaria (histamine → dermal oedema), vasculitis (palpable purpura)
Pilosebaceous unitsAcne, hidradenitis, alopecia
Nerves (C fibres)Itch
SubcutisErythema nodosum

los.text: Describe pathophysiology related to barrier dysfunction, epidemiology and common presentations (diagnostic features)
los.html:
Atopic eczema
  • About 1 in 5 children and 1 in 10 adults in the UK
  • Usually starts before 2
  • Often improves with age.
Pathophysiology
  • Filaggrin loss-of-function mutations and reduced lipids
  • → leaky stratum corneum
  • → ↑ transepidermal water loss, allergen and microbe penetration
  • → Th2 inflammation (IL-4, IL-13; IL-31 drives itch)
  • → S. aureus colonisation
  • → itch–scratch cycle further damages the barrier.
TriggersSoaps and detergents, heat, sweat, wool, stress, infection, house dust mite, pets, teething.
Presentation
Itch (essential), dry skin
Infants: face, scalp and extensor surfaces (nappy area spared)
Older children and adults: flexures (antecubital, popliteal fossae, neck, wrists, ankles)
Acute: erythema, vesicles, weeping, crusting; chronic: lichenification, excoriations, hyperpigmentation
Infraorbital (Dennie–Morgan) folds, hyperlinear palms
Diagnosis (UK Working Party)
  • Itchy skin plus 3 or more of: history of flexural involvement
  • Personal history of asthma/hay fever
  • Generally dry skin
  • Onset under 2
  • Visible flexural eczema.
Other barrier disordersIrritant contact dermatitis (wet work, healthcare hand dermatitis), venous (stasis) eczema, asteatotic eczema (elderly, dry), seborrhoeic dermatitis (Malassezia).
Management
  • Emollients generously and as a soap substitute
  • Topical steroids stepped up and down by severity (once daily, fingertip units)
  • Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) for the face
  • Bandages/wet wraps
  • Sedating antihistamine short-term for sleep
  • Treat infection (flucloxacillin; aciclovir for eczema herpeticum)
  • Phototherapy
  • Systemic (ciclosporin, methotrexate, azathioprine, dupilumab, JAK inhibitors).

los.text: Describe pathophysiology and epidemiology of skin tumours, link to structure and function. Formulate appropriate management plan
sessions: Skin tumours and Benign skin conditions
los.html:
TumourCell / causesFeaturesManagement
Basal cell carcinomaBasal keratinocytes; UV, fair skin, older agePearly papule with rolled edge and telangiectasia, central ulceration ("rodent ulcer"); face; locally invasive, almost never metastasisesSurgical excision (~4 mm margin), Mohs surgery (face), curettage, cryotherapy, imiquimod or PDT for superficial; routine referral
Squamous cell carcinomaKeratinocytes; UV, immunosuppression (transplant), actinic keratoses, chronic wounds and scars (Marjolin's ulcer), HPVRapidly growing, keratotic, tender nodule, may ulcerate; lips, ears, scalp, hands; can metastasiseSuspected cancer referral; excision with margins; radiotherapy
MelanomaMelanocytes; intermittent intense UV (sunburn, especially in childhood), sunbeds, fair skin, many or atypical naevi, family or previous history, immunosuppression
  • ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border irregular, Colour variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution
  • Types: superficial spreading (commonest), nodular (aggressive), lentigo maligna (elderly face), acral lentiginous (palms, soles, nails: darker skin)
  • Suspected cancer referral
  • Excision biopsy (2 mm margin), then wide local excision by Breslow thickness, sentinel node biopsy
  • Immunotherapy (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab), BRAF/MEK inhibitors
Glasgow 7-point checklist(NICE)
  • Major (2 points each): change in size, shape, colour
  • Minor (1 point each): diameter ≥7 mm, inflammation, oozing, change in sensation
  • ≥3 points → suspected cancer referral.
Pre-malignantActinic keratosis (rough scaly patches on sun-exposed skin: 5-FU cream, cryotherapy), Bowen's disease (SCC in situ).
Link to structure
  • Invasion through the basement membrane defines invasive cancer
  • Depth in the dermis (Breslow) determines access to lymphatics and vessels and so prognosis.
PreventionShade 11 am–3 pm, clothing and hats, SPF 30+ with high UVA rating, no sunbeds, skin self-checks.

los.text: Know the epidemiology, pathophysiology and presentation of benign skin tumours.
sessions: Skin tumours and Benign skin conditions
los.html:
Benign tumourFeatures
Seborrhoeic keratosis
  • Very common in older adults
  • "stuck-on", warty, waxy, brown–black
  • Reassure (cryotherapy if irritated).
  • A sudden eruption (Leser–Trélat) can signal internal cancer
Melanocytic naevi (moles)Junctional (flat), compound (raised, pigmented), intradermal (raised, pale); congenital naevi; atypical (dysplastic) naevi raise melanoma risk
DermatofibromaFirm brown nodule on the legs, dimples when pinched; often after an insect bite
Skin tags (acrochordons)Neck, axillae; obesity, diabetes
Lipoma, epidermoid cyst (punctum), pilar cyst (scalp)Soft mobile lump; cyst with central punctum
Cherry angioma (Campbell de Morgan spot)Small red papules, middle age
Pyogenic granulomaRapidly growing, friable red nodule that bleeds; excise for histology (exclude amelanotic melanoma)
Infantile haemangiomaAppears in first weeks, grows for months, then involutes; propranolol if near eyes, airway or ulcerating
KeloidScar tissue extending beyond the wound; darker skin, chest and earlobes
  • Pathophysiology: benign clonal or reactive proliferations that don't invade the basement membrane; most become commoner with age and sun exposure.

los.text: Know the aetiology of pruritus (including systemic causes) which investigations are needed and commence management.
los.html:
Cause of itchExamples
With a rash (dermatological)Eczema, urticaria, scabies, lichen planus, dermatitis herpetiformis, xerosis, pre-bullous pemphigoid, psoriasis
Without a rash (systemic)
  • Cholestasis (PBC, obstruction, pregnancy)
  • CKD (uraemic)
  • Iron deficiency
  • Polycythaemia vera (after a hot bath)
  • Lymphoma (Hodgkin's, with B symptoms)
  • Thyroid disease
  • Diabetes
  • Drugs (opioids)
  • HIV
  • Other malignancy
  • Pregnancy
  • Neuropathic
  • Psychogenic
  • Dry skin in older people
Investigations for generalised itch without a rash
  • FBC (polycythaemia, eosinophilia), ferritin, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, HbA1c, ESR/CRP, LDH, CXR (lymphoma), HIV and hepatitis serology if at risk, urine dip
  • Consider protein electrophoresis
  • Skin scrapings if scabies possible.
Management
  • Treat the cause
  • Emollients, cool environment, avoid irritants and hot showers, menthol in aqueous cream
  • Sedating antihistamine at night (limited benefit except urticaria)
  • Specific: colestyramine (cholestasis), gabapentin and UVB (uraemic), sertraline
  • Scabies: permethrin 5% for the patient and all close contacts at the same time, repeat after 7 days.

los.text: Know cutaneous manifestations of paraneoplasia, autoimmune (vitiligo, alopaecia areata), vascular diseases (ulceration and oedema) and others
los.html:
GroupConditionClues
ParaneoplasticAcanthosis nigricans (malignant type)Velvety dark skin in flexures; gastric adenocarcinoma (also insulin resistance)
DermatomyositisHeliotrope eyelid rash, Gottron's papules, proximal weakness; ovarian, lung, GI cancer
Leser–Trélat signSudden eruption of seborrhoeic keratoses: GI adenocarcinoma
Sweet's syndromePainful red plaques, fever: AML
Necrolytic migratory erythemaGlucagonoma
Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau)Pancreatic cancer
Erythema gyratum repens, acquired ichthyosis, generalised itchLung cancer, lymphoma
AutoimmuneVitiligo
  • Symmetrical depigmented patches (hands, around orifices)
  • T-cell destruction of melanocytes
  • Linked to thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, Addison's
  • Topical steroid or calcineurin inhibitor, NB-UVB, ruxolitinib cream, camouflage, sun protection
Alopecia areataWell-defined bald patches, "exclamation mark" hairs; T-cell attack on follicles; often regrows; steroids, JAK inhibitors
Cutaneous lupusMalar rash sparing nasolabial folds, discoid lesions, photosensitivity
VascularVenous diseaseVaricose eczema, haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis, oedema; venous ulcers in the gaiter area, shallow: compression after checking ABPI
Arterial ulcersPunched out, painful, toes and pressure points, absent pulses
VasculitisPalpable purpura
Pyoderma gangrenosumRapidly enlarging painful ulcer with violaceous undermined edge; IBD, RA; avoid debridement (pathergy)
LymphoedemaNon-pitting swelling, Stemmer's sign, recurrent cellulitis
OthersErythema nodosumTender red shin nodules: sarcoidosis, streptococcal infection, TB, IBD, pregnancy, drugs
Necrobiosis lipoidicaShiny yellow shin plaques: diabetes
Dermatitis herpetiformisItchy vesicles on extensors: coeliac disease
Pretibial myxoedema, xanthomas, spider naeviGraves', hyperlipidaemia, liver disease

los.text: Apply existing knowledge of microbiology to skin and relate to structure and function
los.html:
• Normal flora (S. epidermidis, Cutibacterium acnes, corynebacteria, Malassezia) protects by competition and stimulating antimicrobial peptides
    • ~30% carry S. aureus in the nose.
    • Infection follows breaks in the barrier (eczema, wounds, toe-web tinea, ulcers, oedema).
Depth / structureInfectionOrganismTreatment
EpidermisImpetigo (honey-coloured crusts); bullous impetigo (exfoliative toxin)S. aureus, S. pyogenesLocalised: hydrogen peroxide 1% cream (or fusidic acid); extensive: flucloxacillin
SSSS (children: widespread superficial peeling, Nikolsky positive, mucosae spared)S. aureus toxin cleaving desmoglein 1IV antibiotics
Hair folliclesFolliculitis, boils (furuncles), carbunclesS. aureus (PVL strains: recurrent boils)Drainage, antibiotics
Upper dermis + lymphaticsErysipelas (well-demarcated, raised)S. pyogenesPenicillin/flucloxacillin
Deep dermis + subcutisCellulitis (poorly demarcated, hot, red, swollen)S. pyogenes, S. aureusFlucloxacillin (clarithromycin or doxycycline if penicillin-allergic); mark the edge
FasciaNecrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus, shock)Polymicrobial (type 1) or group A strep (type 2)Emergency surgical debridement + IV antibiotics (including clindamycin)
ViralHSV (grouped vesicles; eczema herpeticum), VZV (chickenpox, dermatomal shingles), HPV (warts), molluscum contagiosum (umbilicated papules), hand, foot and mouth (coxsackie)Aciclovir for HSV/VZV where indicated
Fungal
  • Dermatophytes: tinea corporis (annular, scaly active edge, central clearing), pedis, cruris, capitis, unguium
  • Candida (intertrigo with satellite lesions)
  • Malassezia (pityriasis versicolor, seborrhoeic dermatitis)
Topical terbinafine/azoles; oral terbinafine for nails (confirm with clippings) or griseofulvin/terbinafine for scalp; steroids worsen tinea (tinea incognito)
InfestationsScabies (burrows in finger webs, wrists, genitals; itch worse at night); crusted scabies in the immunosuppressed; head liceSarcoptes scabieiPermethrin 5% whole body, repeat at 7 days, treat all contacts; ivermectin for crusted

los.text: Understand pathophysiology and diagnosis of urticaria, TEN/SJS, drug reactions, blistering, erythroderma, eczema herpeticum
los.html:
ConditionPathophysiologyDiagnosis / key features
UrticariaMast cell degranulation → histamine → dermal oedema (wheals); angioedema = deeper oedema
  • Itchy wheals each lasting <24 h
  • Acute (<6 weeks: infection, food, drugs such as NSAIDs) or chronic (>6 weeks: spontaneous or inducible).
  • Non-sedating antihistamine (up to 4× dose), short oral steroid if severe, omalizumab.
  • ACE inhibitor and hereditary (C1 esterase inhibitor) angioedema are bradykinin-mediated: no wheals, antihistamines don't work
SJS / TENDrug-specific cytotoxic T cells → widespread keratinocyte apoptosis → full-thickness epidermal necrosis
  • 1–4 weeks after a new drug (allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfonamides/co-trimoxazole, NSAIDs, nevirapine)
  • Fever, painful dusky macules → blisters and skin detachment (Nikolsky positive), mucosal erosions (mouth, eyes, genitals)
  • SJS <10% body surface, TEN >30%
  • SCORTEN for prognosis.
  • Stop the drug, burns unit/ICU, fluids, analgesia, wound and eye care
  • Mortality in TEN ~30%
Drug reactionsVarious
  • Morbilliform rash (commonest; amoxicillin in EBV)
  • Fixed drug eruption
  • DRESS (2–8 weeks: fever, facial swelling, rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, hepatitis: anticonvulsants, allopurinol)
  • AGEP (pustules)
  • Photosensitivity (doxycycline, amiodarone, thiazides)
Bullous pemphigoidIgG against hemidesmosome proteins (BP180/230) → subepidermal split
  • Elderly
  • Tense, itchy blisters on red/urticated skin
  • Mucosae rarely
  • Nikolsky negative
  • Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence (linear IgG/C3 at the BMZ)
  • Potent topical steroid (clobetasol), doxycycline, oral steroid
Pemphigus vulgarisIgG against desmoglein 3 → intraepidermal acantholysisMiddle age; flaccid blisters and erosions, mouth first; Nikolsky positive; DIF "chicken-wire" intercellular; oral steroids + rituximab
ErythrodermaInflammation of >90% of the skin → skin failure
  • Causes: eczema, psoriasis, drugs, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
  • Risks: hypothermia, fluid and protein loss, high-output heart failure, infection
  • Admit, emollients, fluids, warmth, treat cause
Eczema herpeticumHSV spreading through eczematous skinClusters of monomorphic punched-out erosions, unwell, febrile: emergency → aciclovir (IV if severe), same-day dermatology, ophthalmology if near the eye

los.text: Know the epidemiology, pathophysiology and diagnosis of acne and rosacea and commence management.
los.html:
Acne vulgarisRosacea
WhoTeenagers (~80–90%), can persistAdults 30–50, fair skin
PathophysiologyAndrogen-driven sebum ↑, follicular hyperkeratinisation (comedones), Cutibacterium acnes, inflammationNeurovascular dysregulation, innate immune activation, Demodex mites
FeaturesComedones (open "blackheads", closed "whiteheads"), papules, pustules, nodules, cysts, scarring; face, back, chestFlushing (alcohol, spicy food, heat, sun), persistent central facial erythema, telangiectasia, papules and pustules without comedones, rhinophyma, ocular (blepharitis, keratitis)
AssociationsPCOS, drugs (steroids, progestogens, lithium, anabolic steroids)
Acne management (NICE NG198)
  • Skin care (non-comedogenic products)
  • 12-week topical combination first: adapalene + benzoyl peroxide, tretinoin + clindamycin or benzoyl peroxide + clindamycin
  • Moderate–severe: add oral lymecycline or doxycycline with topical adapalene/BPO (never antibiotic monotherapy; tetracyclines not in pregnancy or under 12; review at 12 weeks, maximum 6 months)
  • COCP in women
  • Severe, nodular or scarring: refer for isotretinoin (teratogenic: Pregnancy Prevention Programme; dry skin and lips, raised lipids and LFTs, mood changes monitoring; not with tetracyclines).
  • Topical retinoids are avoided in pregnancy.
Rosacea management
  • Avoid triggers, daily SPF
  • Erythema: brimonidine gel
  • Papulopustular: topical ivermectin, azelaic acid or metronidazole
  • Moderate–severe: + oral doxycycline (40 mg MR)
  • Telangiectasia: laser
  • Ocular: lid hygiene, ophthalmology if keratitis.

los.text: Appreciate the challenge of dermatology in the junior doctor setting and how to deal with it.
los.html:
Why it's hard
  • Little undergraduate training
  • Lots of skin problems in inpatients (rashes, drug reactions, cellulitis, leg ulcers, pressure damage, infections)
  • Difficulty describing lesions accurately
  • Recognising emergencies
  • Skin of colour (erythema looks violaceous or darker, harder to see)
  • Limited on-site dermatology.
Strategies
  • Examine systematically and describe with correct terms (distribution, configuration, morphology).
  • Check the drug chart for new drugs (rash in hospital is drug-related until proven otherwise).
  • Know the emergencies: SJS/TEN, DRESS, erythroderma, eczema herpeticum, necrotising fasciitis, meningococcal rash, angioedema/anaphylaxis, pustular psoriasis.
  • Take good clinical photographs (consent, secure devices, follow policy) for advice and guidance/teledermatology.
  • Use reliable resources: BAD patient leaflets, PCDS, DermNet, BNF.
  • Prescribe topicals properly: emollient quantities, steroid potency, fingertip units, duration.
  • Know when to biopsy, refer (suspected cancer pathway) or ask for same-day review.

los.text: Diagnose common inflammatory skin diseases and formulate management
los.html:
ConditionFeaturesManagement
Chronic plaque psoriasis (2–3%)
  • Well-demarcated, salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale on extensors (elbows, knees), scalp, lower back, umbilicus
  • Nail pitting, onycholysis
  • Koebner phenomenon
  • Triggers: streptococcal infection (guttate), stress, trauma, drugs (lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials, steroid withdrawal), alcohol, smoking.
  • Th17/IL-23 driven keratinocyte hyperproliferation
  • Potent topical steroid + vitamin D analogue (calcipotriol) first line (combined, once daily up to 4 weeks)
  • Coal tar, dithranol
  • Scalp: potent steroid
  • Face/flexures: mild steroid or calcineurin inhibitor
  • NB-UVB
  • Systemic: methotrexate (with folic acid; FBC/LFT monitoring), ciclosporin, acitretin, apremilast
  • Biologics (adalimumab, ustekinumab, secukinumab, risankizumab) if severe
Atopic eczemaSee LO 5
Seborrhoeic dermatitisGreasy yellow scale on scalp (dandruff), eyebrows, nasolabial folds, chest; cradle cap; HIV, Parkinson's; MalasseziaKetoconazole shampoo/cream, mild steroid
Contact dermatitisIrritant (commonest; detergents, wet work) or allergic (type IV: nickel, fragrances, rubber, hair dye, preservatives)Avoid the cause, emollients, steroids; patch testing for allergy
Lichen planusPurple, polygonal, planar, pruritic papules with Wickham's striae (wrists); lacy white oral lesionsPotent topical steroid
UrticariaSee LO 11
Hidradenitis suppurativaRecurrent painful nodules, abscesses and sinus tracts in axillae and groin; smoking, obesityTetracyclines, adalimumab, surgery
  • Topical steroid ladder (UK): mild hydrocortisone 1%
    • → moderate clobetasone butyrate 0.05% (Eumovate)
    • → potent betamethasone valerate 0.1% (Betnovate), mometasone (Elocon)
    • → very potent clobetasol propionate 0.05% (Dermovate).
    • 1 fingertip unit (~0.5 g) covers two adult palms.
    • Side effects: atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis, tinea incognito, rarely adrenal suppression.
    • Emollients: 250–500 g/week for adults
    • paraffin-based products are a fire risk on fabrics.

los.text: Formulate the diagnosis and management plan on virtual cases.
los.html:
Virtual caseLikely diagnosisPlan
Child with asthma, itchy flexural rash, dry skinAtopic eczemaEmollients, topical steroid, treat infection
70-year-old with a pearly nodule with rolled edge on the noseBCCRoutine dermatology referral, excision or Mohs
Changing mole, irregular border and colours, 8 mmMelanomaSuspected cancer referral
Hot, swollen, tender, poorly demarcated leg with feverCellulitisFlucloxacillin, mark the edge, elevate, consider DVT
Painful dusky skin, blisters and mouth ulcers 2 weeks after starting lamotrigineSJS/TENStop the drug, emergency admission
Elderly woman with tense itchy blistersBullous pemphigoidBiopsy with DIF, clobetasol
Ring-shaped scaly patch with clear centreTinea corporisScrapings, topical terbinafine
Itchy burrows in finger webs, family also itchyScabiesPermethrin for everyone, repeat at 7 days
Silvery plaques on elbows, nail pitting, sore jointsPsoriasis ± psoriatic arthritisSteroid + vitamin D analogue, rheumatology
Teenager with comedones and pustulesAcneTopical combination therapy
45-year-old with flushing, central facial papules, no comedonesRosaceaTrigger avoidance, topical ivermectin
Child with honey-crusted lesions around the mouthImpetigoHydrogen peroxide cream, school exclusion until crusted or 48 h after antibiotics
  • Approach to every case: history → describe → differential → investigations → management → safety-net and follow-up.

los.text: Elicit a focused neurological history from a patient with speech impairment, using adapted communication strategies as needed
sessions: Neuro history and exams- cranial, arms and legs with dysarthric patient
los.html:
• First identify the type of speech problem: dysarthria (articulation: understands and chooses words normally), dysphasia (language: expressive, receptive or both) or dysphonia (voice).
    • This decides how to adapt.
Adapted communication
Quiet room, face the patient, allow extra time, don't rush or finish their sentences
Short, simple, closed (yes/no) questions, one at a time
Use gestures, writing, pictures, communication boards or the patient's own aids
Check understanding by summarising back; ask them to nod or point
Receptive dysphasia: simple language, gestures, demonstrate; check comprehension with simple commands
Expressive dysphasia: closed questions; let them try writing (may also be impaired)
Collateral history from family/carers (with consent); SALT involvement; don't assume cognitive impairment
  • Content: onset (sudden: stroke; gradual: MND, tumour, Parkinson's)
    • progression
    • fluctuation/fatigability (myasthenia)
    • associated symptoms (weakness, numbness, swallowing problems, choking, drooling, weight loss, visual disturbance, headache, memory)
    • vascular risk factors (AF, hypertension, smoking, diabetes)
    • PMH
    • drugs
    • alcohol
    • family history
    • function and impact
    • ICE.

los.text: Perform a structured neurological examination and propose additional relevant examinations (e.g. cranial nerve, cognitive, or speech assessments) based on clinical findings
sessions: Neuro history and exams- cranial, arms and legs with dysarthric patient
los.html:
Structured neurological examination
General: alertness, posture, facial asymmetry, wasting, fasciculations, tremor
Speech: fluency, comprehension (simple commands), naming, repetition, reading, writing; articulation ("baby hippopotamus"); voice
  • Cranial nerves: especially V (jaw jerk)
  • VII (UMN vs LMN facial weakness)
  • IX/X (palate, gag, cough)
  • XII (tongue wasting, fasciculation, deviation)
  • Eye movements (fatigable ptosis)
Limbs: tone, power (MRC), reflexes, plantars, coordination, sensation; pronator drift
Gait
Additional examinations to propose
  • Cognitive assessment (MoCA, ACE-III)
  • Bedside swallow screen
  • Fatigability tests (sustained upgaze, counting to 50)
  • Fundoscopy (papilloedema)
  • Cardiovascular exam (AF, carotid bruits, murmurs) in suspected stroke
  • Visual fields.
InvestigationsCT/MRI brain, bloods (glucose, FBC, U&E, lipids, HbA1c), ECG, AChR antibodies, EMG, SALT assessment.

los.text: Present the findings of the neurological history and examination using structured and concise medical terminology
sessions: Neuro history and exams- cranial, arms and legs with dysarthric patient
los.html:
Structure
  • Who and why
  • → key positive history
  • → key positive and relevant negative findings
  • → summary
  • → localisation
  • → differential
  • → next steps.
Example
  • "Mr X, a 68-year-old with atrial fibrillation not anticoagulated, presented with sudden-onset difficulty speaking 2 hours ago.
  • Examination showed an expressive dysphasia with intact comprehension
  • a right UMN facial weakness (forehead sparing)
  • Right pronator drift
  • MRC 4/5 power in the right arm with brisk reflexes and an upgoing plantar.
  • Sensation and coordination were normal.
  • In summary, these findings localise to the left frontal lobe/left MCA territory, most likely an acute ischaemic stroke.
  • I'd like an urgent CT head with CT angiography to assess for thrombolysis and thrombectomy."
TerminologyDysarthria vs dysphasia (expressive/receptive), UMN/LMN, MRC grades, hyper-/hyporeflexia, Babinski, clonus, ataxia, dysdiadochokinesia, fasciculations, sensory level.

los.text: Formulate a list of differential diagnoses based on the neurological history and examination findings
sessions: Neuro history and exams- cranial, arms and legs with dysarthric patient
los.html:
PatternDifferentials
Sudden dysphasia ± hemiparesisStroke/TIA (dominant MCA), haemorrhage, hypoglycaemia, Todd's paresis after a seizure, migraine aura
Progressive dysarthria, fasciculating tongue, mixed UMN/LMN signsMotor neurone disease (bulbar onset)
Fatigable dysarthria/dysphagia with ptosis, diplopiaMyasthenia gravis
Quiet, monotonous speech with bradykinesiaParkinson's disease
Slurred, scanning speech with ataxia and nystagmusCerebellar: MS, alcohol, stroke, drugs (phenytoin)
Progressive word-finding difficultyPrimary progressive aphasia (frontotemporal dementia), Alzheimer's, tumour
Slow spastic speech, brisk jaw jerk, emotional labilityPseudobulbar palsy (bilateral strokes, MS, MND)
HoarsenessRecurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, laryngeal cancer
Facial weakness affecting articulationBell's palsy
OthersBrain tumour, encephalitis, MS, intoxication, myopathy, functional

los.text: Define and explain commonly used dermatological descriptive terms (e.g., macule, papule, pustule) to accurately describe skin findings
los.html:
TermDefinition (size cut-offs vary between sources)
MaculeFlat area of colour change, <1 cm (≥1 cm = patch)
PapuleRaised solid lesion <1 cm (≥1 cm = nodule, deeper)
PlaqueRaised, flat-topped lesion ≥1 cm (e.g. psoriasis)
VesicleFluid-filled blister <0.5 cm (≥0.5 cm = bulla)
PustulePus-filled lesion
WhealTransient, itchy, oedematous swelling (urticaria)
ScaleFlakes of stratum corneum
CrustDried serum, blood or pus
ErosionPartial loss of epidermis (heals without scarring)
UlcerLoss of epidermis and dermis (may scar)
FissureLinear crack
ExcoriationScratch mark
LichenificationThickened skin with exaggerated markings from rubbing
AtrophyThinning (e.g. steroid use)
PurpuraNon-blanching bleeding into the skin (petechiae <2 mm, ecchymosis = bruise)
TelangiectasiaVisible small dilated blood vessels
ComedonePlugged pilosebaceous follicle
BurrowLinear track (scabies)
  • Also describe: distribution (symmetrical, flexural, extensor, dermatomal, sun-exposed, acral)
    • configuration (annular, linear, grouped, target, discoid)
    • colour
    • border (well- or ill-defined)
    • surface
    • and palpation (texture, temperature, tenderness, blanching).

los.text: Perform a systematic dermatological examination, identifying relevant skin lesions, and present findings in a structured and clear manner
los.html:
1Introduce, consent, chaperone if needed; good natural light; expose all the skin (with dignity), as patients often have unnoticed lesions.
2. General inspectionDistribution, number, symmetry.
3. Each lesionSite, size (measure), shape, colour, border, surface, morphology (primary lesion + secondary changes), configuration.
4. PalpateTexture, temperature, tenderness, depth, mobility, blanching (glass test).
5Hair, nails, mucous membranes (mouth, eyes, genitals if relevant); lymph nodes (tumours).
6Dermatoscopy if trained; photograph with consent.
  • Presenting: "On examination there are multiple well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on the extensor surfaces of both elbows and knees, with nail pitting.
    • No pustules or joint swelling.
    • This is consistent with chronic plaque psoriasis."

los.text: Identify and classify common dermatological conditions (e.g., eczema, psoriasis, basal cell carcinoma) and recognise characteristic skin lesions
los.html:
CategoryConditionsCharacteristic lesion
InflammatoryEczemaIll-defined, red, dry, scaly patches, excoriations, lichenification, flexural
PsoriasisWell-demarcated salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale, extensors, nail pitting
Acne / rosaceaComedones + papules/pustules / central facial erythema without comedones
Urticaria, lichen planusTransient wheals / purple polygonal papules
InfectionImpetigo, cellulitis, shingles, tineaGolden crusts / hot poorly demarcated swelling / dermatomal vesicles / annular scaly active edge

Pre-malignantActinic keratosis, Bowen'sRough scaly patch on sun-exposed skin
MalignantBCCPearly papule, rolled edge, telangiectasia, central ulcer

los.text: Perform a swab collection appropriately, ensuring the correct technique, type of swab and site
los.html:
StepDetail
IndicationsSuspected bacterial infection (impetigo, infected eczema, wound infection, discharge), viral (HSV/VZV: vesicle fluid for PCR), MRSA screening (nose, groin/perineum, wounds), STIs
Correct swab
  • Bacterial: swab in transport medium (charcoal/Amies) for culture
  • Viral: swab into viral transport medium for PCR
  • Fungi: send skin scrapings, hair or nail clippings, not swabs
PreparationIdentity, explain, consent, hand hygiene, gloves, ANTT; check the swab expiry
Wound swab
  • Clean off surface debris with sterile saline (not antiseptic)
  • Use the Levine technique: rotate the swab over ~1 cm² of viable tissue with enough pressure to express fluid
  • Avoid necrotic tissue
  • Moisten a dry wound swab with saline
  • Pus: aspirate with a syringe if possible
VesicleDe-roof the blister and rub the base firmly to collect cells and fluid
MRSA screenMoisten, rotate inside both anterior nares, then groin/perineum (separate swabs per local policy)
After
  • Put it in the medium
  • Label at the bedside (name, DOB, number, site, date and time)
  • Complete the request with clinical details and antibiotics
  • Send promptly
  • Document

los.text: To be able to identify the layers of the skin histologically and link with function
los.html:
LayerHistologyFunctionLinked disease
EpidermisKeratinised stratified squamous epithelium; avascularBarrier against water loss, microbes, UV
↳ Stratum basaleSingle row of dividing keratinocytes on the basement membrane; melanocytes, Merkel cellsRenewal (~4 weeks to reach the surface), pigment, touchBasal cell carcinoma; melanoma (melanocytes)
↳ Stratum spinosumCells joined by desmosomes ("prickles"); Langerhans cellsStrength; antigen presentationPemphigus (antibodies to desmosomes); squamous cell carcinoma
↳ Stratum granulosumKeratohyalin granules; lipid lamellar granulesWaterproof lipid barrierIchthyosis, eczema (filaggrin)
↳ Stratum lucidumClear layer, thick skin only (palms, soles)Friction resistance
↳ Stratum corneumDead flattened keratin-filled cellsMain barrier, shed constantlyPsoriasis (thickened, nuclei retained: parakeratosis)
Basement membrane / dermo-epidermal junctionHemidesmosomes, rete ridgesAnchors epidermisBullous pemphigoid (antibodies to hemidesmosomes)
Dermis: papillaryLoose connective tissue in dermal papillae; capillary loops, Meissner's corpusclesNourishes epidermis, fine touch
Dermis: reticularDense irregular connective tissue (collagen I, elastin); hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands, Pacinian corpuscles, vessels, nervesStrength, elasticity, thermoregulation (sweat, vessels)Ageing and UV damage (elastosis), striae, Ehlers–Danlos
Hypodermis (subcutis)Adipose tissue, larger vesselsInsulation, energy store, cushioningCellulitis spreads here; panniculitis
Thick vs thin skin
  • Thick skin (palms and soles) has a stratum lucidum, a thick corneum and no hair follicles
  • Thin skin has hair and sebaceous glands.
GlandsEccrine sweat glands (everywhere, thermoregulation), apocrine (axilla, groin; open into hair follicles), sebaceous (sebum; acne).
Mnemonic for the epidermis from deep to superficial: "British Soldiers Get Lots of Cash".
